screens.title: Optimizing Performance & Debugging in UE5
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn a practical workflow for finding and fixing performance problems in Unreal Engine using the tools already included with the editor and by applying targeted C++ techniques. By the end you’ll be able to identify real bottlenecks, apply fixes guided by data, and avoid common traps like premature optimization or missing debug symbols.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical skills you'll use while developing and shipping a game in Unreal Engine. Second, you'll apply targeted C++ optimizations: improving cache locality, lowering allocations, and removing unnecessary per-frame work. These techniques directly reduce C P U and memory overhead. Third, you'll adopt a debugging workflow with Visual Studio or Rider: attaching the debugger, setting conditional breakpoints, stepping through code, and inspecting the call stack. Finally, you'll master UE_LOG for structured logging, choosing categories and verbosity levels so logs help diagnosis without flooding release builds. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint to make the competency easier to remember when you are in the editor. These skills matter because they let you find the true cause of slowdowns and fix them safely, preserving game correctness while improving performance.

screens.title: Stat Commands: Fast runtime checks
screens.narratorSegment: Stat commands are your fastest first step when performance feels off. Typing commands like Stat FPS, Stat Unit, or Stat Game into the in-editor console gives you instant, low-overhead measurements that tell you whether the frame rate, game thread, or G P U is the likely cause. For example, Stat Unit breaks frame time into Game, Draw, G P U, and RHI; if G P U time is dominant, optimizing C P U code won't help. Stat Game lists per-feature timings such as actor ticks, AI, and animation; a high value for an actor tick points you to which code to profile further. A common misconception is to trust perceived slowness: a connected profiler might show the real culprit is the render thread or G P U. Use Stat to triage quickly and avoid premature optimization. Concrete example: add the provided MyPerformanceActor to your level, run Stat Unit, and watch game thread timing rise — that confirms Tick is problematic. Key takeaway: Stat commands are triage tools — use them to form a hypothesis before deeper captures. Stat Commands: Fast runtime checks means run stat unit and stat game first to determine which thread or subsystem is causing slow frames before deeper profiling.. In practical terms, use console stat commands to get immediate timing and thread breakdowns.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Stat Commands
Definition
Stat Commands
Console commands that report runtime metrics for quick diagnosis. They are low overhead and ideal for triage.
Stat FPS — shows frame rate and frame time.
Stat Unit — splits frame time into Game, Draw, GPU, RHI.
Stat Game — shows game-thread breakdown including actor ticks and AI.
Concrete Example
Add the MyPerformanceActor to a level and run the editor. Open the console and type Stat Unit. If Game time spikes above Draw and GPU, the actor's Tick is likely the culprit. This gives a hypothesis to confirm with Session Frontend.
Process
Step-by-step triage using Stat commands
1
Run Stat FPS
Confirm whether the symptom is a general frame-rate drop.
2
Run Stat Unit
See Game vs Draw vs GPU to identify the dominant subsystem.
3
Run Stat Game
Look for high actor tick times or AI entries that point to specific code areas.
Common Mistake
Assuming visible stutter equals CPU time. Stat Unit often shows that GPU or Render Thread is the actual bottleneck; optimize where the data points you to.

screens.title: Session Frontend: capture and inspect
screens.narratorSegment: Session Frontend is the next step after Stat triage. It records detailed traces over time so you can inspect C P U and G P U work, draw calls, and memory usage. Start by opening Session Frontend from Window → Developer Tools → Session Frontend, connect to your running editor instance, and begin a capture while reproducing the performance issue. The capture collects per-thread timings: Game Thread, Render Thread, RHI Thread, and G P U samples. Use the C P U usage view to sort by self-time or total time to find the function dominating the profile. Drill into the call stack to see which higher-level code called that function. For example, if you find AMyPerformanceActor::Tick has a high self-time, you now have a precise target. A common misconception is to chase high total time functions without checking self-time; prioritize functions with large self-time reductions after optimization. Concrete example: capture a 5–10 second trace while the heavy actor runs, then search for Tick entries and examine the call stack to verify where the heavy loop executes. End by exporting a short clip or saving the capture for comparison after fixes.

screens.title: Cache Locality: the CPU reality
screens.narratorSegment: Cache locality is a foundational C++ optimization principle you can use to improve C P U efficiency without changing algorithms. Modern CPUs read memory in cache lines. When data that will be used together is stored contiguously, the C P U can load it into cache once and reuse it. This drastically reduces memory access latency compared to chasing pointers that scatter data across memory. In Unreal C++ a common pattern is preferring a TArray of structs over a TArray of pointers to structs when you iterate frequently, because a struct array is contiguous. Concrete example: if you store particle states in a TArray and loop to update them, you get sequential memory access. If instead you store pointers to heap-allocated particle objects, each dereference may miss the cache. A misconception is thinking cache locality only matters for huge systems; in tight per-frame loops it can change your frame time measurably. Key practice: profile hot loops, then consider re-laying out data for contiguous access to reduce cache misses. Cache Locality: the CPU reality means use contiguous containers like tarray of structs to improve cache hit rates in frequently iterated code.. In practical terms, arrange data so related items are contiguous to improve cache hits.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Cache Locality
Concept
Cache Locality
Place frequently accessed, related data contiguously so CPU caches can load and reuse it efficiently.
Why it matters: Reduced cache misses lower memory latency and improve per-frame timings in hot loops.
How to detect: Use Session Frontend to find hot loops, then inspect data access patterns in code.
Quick win: Replace scattered pointers with contiguous arrays for update loops.
Analogy & Example
Think of cache as a small workbench. If all tools you need are on the bench, you avoid trips to the warehouse. In code: iterate a TArray of structs rather than following pointers to heap objects.
Common Mistake
Rewriting an algorithm before checking memory layout. Cache fixes are lower risk and often give immediate gains for tight loops.

screens.title: Reducing allocations & Object Pooling
screens.narratorSegment: Frequent allocations and deallocations are expensive and can fragment memory or add allocator overhead, especially in tight loops or when many small objects are created per frame. Instead of constructing and destroying objects continuously, object pooling reuses pre-allocated items. For example, projectiles or particles that are spawned and destroyed often benefit from a pool: allocate N objects up front and reuse them by resetting state. This reduces calls to the allocator and keeps memory usage stable. Another practical technique is to prefer stack or contiguous allocations where lifetime and size allow, and use smart pointers like MakeShared selectively rather than in hot loops. A common misconception is that garbage will be cleaned quickly; allocator cost still hits frame timings. Concrete example: change code that calls MakeUnique each spawn into a system that checks out an object from a pool and returns it on deactivate. After pooling, re-profile with Session Frontend to confirm reduced allocator time in C P U traces. Key takeaway: reduce runtime allocations on hot paths to lower frame variance and improve stability. Reducing allocations & Object Pooling means use object pools for frequently created and destroyed instances to avoid allocator overhead and memory fragmentation.. In practical terms, avoid per-frame allocations; reuse memory for frequently created objects.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Allocations & Pooling
Comparison
Per-frame allocation vs Object Pool
Per-frame allocation hits allocator repeatedly. Pooling reuses objects to avoid that cost.
Per-frame allocation: expensive, can fragment memory, causes frame spikes.
Object pooling: steady allocation cost, low runtime overhead, predictable frames.
Concrete Example
For frequently spawned projectiles, allocate a pool at BeginPlay. On spawn, mark an element active and reset state; on deactivate, return it to the pool. Then re-profile to see allocator time drop.
Pro Tip
Keep the pool size configurable and monitor usage. Oversized pools waste memory; undersized pools can lead to creation fallback paths you wanted to avoid.

screens.title: Avoid unnecessary per-frame computations
screens.narratorSegment: Per-frame computations are tempting because Tick is easy to use, but unnecessary work in Tick is a common source of slowdowns. Ask whether the computation truly must run every frame. If the value changes rarely, compute it on demand or run it every N frames. If it's independent of frame rate, run it in a timer or a non-tick function. You can also disable ticking by setting PrimaryActorTick. bCanEverTick to false when updates aren't required. A concrete example from the starter actor: heavy trigonometric math inside Tick that repeats every frame can be moved to run once or every tenth frame, or computed asynchronously if appropriate. One misconception is that splitting work across frames always helps; it helps only if the work can be distributed without changing game semantics. After making a change, re-run Stat Unit and capture a Session Frontend trace to verify that Game thread time decreases. Key takeaway: reduce per-frame work by moving calculations to less frequent events or disabling Tick entirely when possible. Avoid unnecessary per-frame computations means only put truly frame-dependent work in tick. prefer timers, events, or conditional execution for expensive calculations.. In practical terms, don't do work every tick; move work to events or lower frequency updates.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Question every Tick
keyIdea.text: Only put truly frame-dependent work in Tick. Prefer timers, events, or conditional execution for expensive calculations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Tick Policy
Definition & Strategy
Avoid unnecessary Tick work
Evaluate if a computation must run every frame. Use conditional execution, timers, or event-driven signals to reduce per-frame load.
A
Move to events
If a value changes on input or collision, compute it when the event occurs rather than every Tick.
B
Frame-skipping
Perform heavy work every N frames using GetWorld()->GetFrameNumber() % N == 0 to spread cost.
C
Disable Tick
If the actor never needs per-frame updates, set PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = false and call a function when needed.
Example
Change the heavy loop in MyPerformanceActor::Tick to only run when GetWorld()->GetFrameNumber() % 10 == 0. Re-profile to confirm lower game thread usage.
Key Takeaway
Every Tick entry increases game-thread cost. Move or reduce frequency for heavy work to improve frame stability.

screens.title: Const correctness & compiler help
screens.narratorSegment: Const correctness is both a correctness and an optimization aid. Marking functions and parameters as const communicates intent, makes A P I contracts clearer, and can help the compiler produce better code in optimized builds. When you promise not to mutate data you enable safer reasoning about side effects, and you often let the optimizer perform more aggressive inlining or reordering. Use const references to avoid unnecessary copies of large structs passed into functions. A practical example: change a function that takes a large struct by value into taking const MyStruct& to remove a copy per call in a hot loop. Keep in mind this is not a substitute for measuring: while const can reduce copies, moving to contiguous data and reducing allocations are often larger wins. A common misconception is over-using const everywhere expecting huge performance gains; const helps correctness and can reduce some overhead, but profiling remains the source of truth. Key takeaway: use const for clarity and to remove accidental copies in hot code paths. Const correctness & compiler help means const references and const methods reduce accidental copies and help maintain clear, optimizable code in hot paths.. In practical terms, use const and clear interfaces so the compiler can optimize and you reduce bugs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
Const correctness
Mark functions and parameters const to prevent unintended mutation and avoid needless copies, aiding both correctness and optimization.
Example: pass large structs as const references to avoid a copy per call in hot loops.
Why it matters: fewer copies reduce CPU and memory overhead and make intent explicit for future maintainers.
Common Mistake
Treating const as an optimization magic. Use it primarily for correctness and to remove copies; verify with profiling for measurable gains.
Pro Tip
Combined with contiguous layouts and reduced allocations, const usage helps keep hot code paths tight and predictable.

screens.title: Starter Actor: find the bottleneck
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the starter AMyPerformanceActor to understand why it shows up in profiling. The header defines NumIterations defaulting to one million, and Tick is enabled in the constructor. In Tick the actor performs a loop from zero to NumIterations, accumulating a result using trigonometric functions. This loop is deterministic work and costs C P U every frame. When you profile, the Game thread will show a large self-time for AMyPerformanceActor::Tick. A common misconception is that printing the result is the bottleneck; often the math or loop itself consumes the time. Concrete debugging steps: add a small UE_LOG call commented out to avoid log spam; instead, profile first to measure. Then set a conditional breakpoint inside Tick and run a DebugGame Editor build to step through and inspect the loop variables. The practical fixes are shown in subsequent lessons: reduce NumIterations, only run every N frames, or disable Tick and run the computation on demand. After a change, reprofile to confirm improvement. In practical terms, walk through the provided myperformanceactor code and identify the heavy loop.. keyIdea.text: The large NumIterations loop in Tick is a predictable cause of game-thread time; profile to confirm and then reduce frequency or iterations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Starter Actor
Header & Implementation
Starter code defines NumIterations and performs a heavy loop in Tick. Keep the code visible so you can scan it while profiling.
// MyPerformanceActor.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Actor.h"
#include "MyPerformanceActor.generated.h"

UCLASS()
class YOURGAME_API AMyPerformanceActor : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:    
    AMyPerformanceActor();

protected:
    virtual void BeginPlay() override;

public:    
    virtual void Tick(float DeltaTime) override;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, Category = "Performance")
    int32 NumIterations = 1000000; // 1 million iterations
};
Implementation excerpt
// MyPerformanceActor.cpp
#include "MyPerformanceActor.h"

AMyPerformanceActor::AMyPerformanceActor()
{
    PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
}

void AMyPerformanceActor::BeginPlay()
{
    Super::BeginPlay();
}

void AMyPerformanceActor::Tick(float DeltaTime)
{
    Super::Tick(DeltaTime);

    // Simulate a heavy computation
    float Result = 0.0f;
    for (int32 i = 0; i < NumIterations; ++i)
    {
        Result += FMath::Sin(i * 0.001f) * FMath::Cos(i * 0.002f);
    }
    // UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("Heavy computation result: %f"), Result); // Optional: use for debugging
}
Check your understanding
If Session Frontend shows high self-time in Tick, what are three immediate options to reduce its per-frame cost? (Reduce iterations, run less often, or disable Tick and run on demand.)

screens.title: Debugging with Visual Studio or Rider
screens.narratorSegment: Debugging C++ in Unreal requires the right build configuration and workflow. Always use DebugGame Editor or Development Editor builds when you need to step through code; Release builds strip symbols and prevent meaningful stepping. To start, attach your IDE debugger to the Unreal Editor process or to a standalone game. Set breakpoints at suspected locations; conditional breakpoints reduce noise by only breaking when a condition is true. Use Step Over to execute the current line, Step Into to dive into called functions, and Step Out to return. Watch windows let you monitor variable values across steps, and the call stack shows the sequence of functions that led to the current point — this is essential when investigating crashes or unexpected states. A common error is debugging the wrong build configuration or forgetting to rebuild after code changes, which leads to mismatched symbols. Concrete example: set a conditional breakpoint inside the heavy Tick to break when i == 0 or when Result is NaN, then step through a few iterations to confirm behavior. After fixing logic, re-run profiler to verify performance and correctness.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › IDE Debugging
Workflow
Attach, Break, Inspect
Attach your IDE to the running editor process, set conditional breakpoints, and use step commands and watches to inspect execution and state.
Build configuration
Use DebugGame Editor or Development Editor for symbols. Release builds remove debug information and make stepping impossible.
Breakpoints & stepping
Set conditional breakpoints to limit stops. Use Step Into, Step Over, and Step Out to navigate execution flow carefully.
Watches & Call Stack
Use watches to observe variables and the call stack to trace the code path that led to the current execution point.
Concrete Example
Set a conditional breakpoint in Tick: break when GetWorld()->GetFrameNumber() % 100 == 0 or when Result is NaN. Step to inspect loop variables for incorrect math or overflow, then fix and re-run profiler to measure change.
Common Mistake
Trying to debug a Release build. If symbols mismatch, rebuild in DebugGame and attach again to get accurate stepping and variable inspection.

screens.title: UE_LOG: structured logging and verbosity
screens.narratorSegment: UE_LOG is the recommended way to emit structured messages in Unreal C++. Unlike ad-hoc prints, UE_LOG supports log categories and verbosity levels so you can filter and control output both in the editor and in standalone logs. Define a custom category with DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY_STATIC to group messages from a subsystem, then use verbosity such as Error, Warning, Display, Log, Verbose, or VeryVerbose to mark importance. For infrequent issues, Verbose or VeryVerbose is appropriate; these levels are commonly ignored in shipping configurations to avoid performance cost and log noise. Example usage: UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("My variable value: %f"), MyVariable); or define a category and log there. A common mistake is leaving heavy logging enabled in hot loops; logging itself can slow your game and flood storage. Use UE_LOG sparingly in hot paths or gate it behind conditional checks. Finally, logs appear in the Output Log and saved game logs, making them invaluable for diagnosing crashes that are hard to reproduce in the editor. UE_LOG: structured logging and verbosity means define categories and choose verbosity levels so logs help diagnosis without creating performance overhead in critical paths.. In practical terms, use ue_log with categories and verbosity to produce useful, filterable logs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › UE_LOG Best Practices
How to use
UE_LOG with categories
Define categories and choose verbosity to keep logs useful and filterable. Avoid heavy logging in hot loops.
// Define a category
DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY_STATIC(MyPerfLog, Log, All);

// Use the log
UE_LOG(MyPerfLog, Verbose, TEXT("Iteration %d result: %f"), i, Result);
Practical guidance
Use Verbose for detailed traces you only enable during deep debugging. Use Warning or Error for issues that should be visible by default. Turn off or gate Verbose logs in production builds to avoid overhead.
Common Pitfall
Leaving high-volume logs unguarded in a hot loop can itself create performance problems and large log files. Always re-profile after adding logs if they run frequently.

screens.title: Profile → Optimize → Re-profile
screens.narratorSegment: This guided activity shows the essential loop: profile, change one thing, then re-profile to verify improvement. Start by placing several MyPerformanceActor instances in the level and run the editor. Use the console to run Stat Unit and Stat Game and note baseline timings. Next open Session Frontend and capture a short trace while the actors run; find AMyPerformanceActor::Tick in the C P U view. Choose one optimization to test: reduce NumIterations, only run the loop every X frames, or disable Tick and run on demand. Implement only that single change and rebuild. Run the same capture sequence again and compare the before and after captures: look for reduced self-time in Tick and lower game-thread time in Stat Unit. This one-change-at-a-time approach isolates cause and effect and prevents accidental regressions. A common beginner mistake is applying several optimizations at once and not knowing which one produced the benefit. End the exercise by restoring the original code and trying a different optimization path to compare trade-offs. Profile → Optimize → Re-profile means always re-profile after a targeted change. comparing traces proves which change produced the improvement.. keyIdea.title: One change, measure result
keyIdea.text: Always re-profile after a targeted change. Comparing traces proves which change produced the improvement.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Lab Workflow
Step-by-step
  1. Place several MyPerformanceActor instances in a level and run the editor to collect baseline Stat Unit and Stat Game readings.
  2. Open Session Frontend and record a 5–10 second capture reproducing the frame drop.
  3. Identify AMyPerformanceActor::Tick in the CPU view and note its self-time.
  4. Make a single optimization (reduce NumIterations, run every N frames, or disable Tick and run on demand).
  5. Rebuild, re-run the same capture sequence, and compare traces and Stat outputs to confirm improvement.
Reflection
Which change reduced self-time the most? Did any change affect correctness or behavior? If so, adjust your approach and re-test.
Key Takeaway
Measure before and after to know which optimization actually improved frame time. Data prevents wasted effort and regressions.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the core concepts you should retain. First, Stat commands provide immediate triage information — use Stat FPS, Stat Unit, and Stat Game to spot which subsystem needs attention. Second, Session Frontend gives function-level timings and call stacks so you can find hot functions and understand why they are expensive. Third, cache locality matters: contiguous data access reduces cache misses and is especially important for tight per-frame loops. Fourth, reduce allocations by using object pools for frequently created objects to avoid allocator overhead. Fifth, avoid unnecessary computations in Tick; prefer events, timers, or lower-frequency updates. Sixth, use const correctness to avoid accidental copies and make code clearer. Seventh, debug with the appropriate build configurations and use breakpoints, stepping, watches, and the call stack to inspect runtime problems. Finally, use UE_LOG with categories and verbosity to produce structured, filterable logs. Keep profiling-driven changes small and re-verify with captures.

Stat Commands
Quick runtime checks like Stat Unit and Stat Game for triage without heavy capture overhead.

Detailed captures for CPU/GPU timings and call stacks to find hot functions precisely.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three practical reminders to use immediately. First, measure before you change: start with Stat and then capture Session Frontend; targeting the wrong subsystem wastes time. Second, optimize memory and frequency: prefer contiguous data and reduce allocations, and move heavy work out of Tick or execute it less often. Third, debug and log wisely: attach a DebugGame Editor build to step through code, use conditional breakpoints and watch windows, and use UE_LOG categories with Verbose levels for deep traces that can be filtered. These three habits — measure, change small, and verify — prevent wasted effort and regressions while improving performance reliably. What to Remember means adopt a disciplined cycle: profile to identify, change one thing guided by data, and re-profile to confirm the win.. In practical terms, three quick cards to carry into your next profiling session. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Final Reminders
Measure First
Run Stat then Session Frontend to find the true bottleneck before changing code.
Change Small
Make one targeted change at a time—reduce iterations, change tick policy, or add pooling—and measure its effect.
Verify with Tools
Re-run Stat and Session Frontend after each change, and use IDE debugging and UE_LOG to confirm correctness.
These habits help you reliably find and fix performance issues without introducing regressions. Keep profiling and keep the fixes measurable.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn a practical workflow for finding and fixing performance problems in Unreal Engine using the tools already included with the editor and by applying targeted C++ techniques. We begin with fast checks using the console Stat commands to spot obvious stalls and then move into deeper captures with Session Frontend so you can inspect threads, function timings, and call stacks. You will also learn concrete C++ strategies — cache-friendly data layout, reducing runtime allocations, and avoiding unnecessary per-frame work — that actually move the profiler needle. Debugging practices come next: attaching Visual Studio or Rider, breakpoints, stepping, and using UE_LOG with appropriate verbosity so logs are useful without overwhelming a build. Throughout, you’ll run a small hands-on example actor that intentionally runs heavy work in Tick, profile it, and apply fixes to see measurable improvements. By the end you’ll be able to identify real bottlenecks, apply fixes guided by data, and avoid common traps like premature optimization or missing debug symbols.

These learning objectives map to practical skills you'll use while developing and shipping a game in Unreal Engine. First, you will learn to use Stat commands and Session Frontend to find where time is spent in your game. This is about reading the numbers, not guessing. Second, you'll apply targeted C++ optimizations: improving cache locality, lowering allocations, and removing unnecessary per-frame work. These techniques directly reduce C P U and memory overhead. Third, you'll adopt a debugging workflow with Visual Studio or Rider: attaching the debugger, setting conditional breakpoints, stepping through code, and inspecting the call stack. Finally, you'll master UE_LOG for structured logging, choosing categories and verbosity levels so logs help diagnosis without flooding release builds. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint to make the competency easier to remember when you are in the editor. These skills matter because they let you find the true cause of slowdowns and fix them safely, preserving game correctness while improving performance.

This secondary objectives slide breaks the learning path into Bloom-style stages so you can see how the skills build. First you will learn to run and read Stat commands — a remember and understand step to get immediate feedback on frame rate and thread timings. Next you will understand how to capture and inspect a Session Frontend trace, locating expensive functions and threads. Then you will apply C++ changes guided by the profile, such as reordering data and pooling objects, which is an apply-level skill that produces measurable improvements. Finally you will master verification: using your IDE and logs to prove the behavior and performance are fixed. Each stage includes a small mnemonic to keep the workflow in mind when you are under time pressure. This structure helps avoid the common trap of optimizing without data, because the bloom progression forces you to measure before and after every change.

Stat commands are your fastest first step when performance feels off. Typing commands like Stat FPS, Stat Unit, or Stat Game into the in-editor console gives you instant, low-overhead measurements that tell you whether the frame rate, game thread, or G P U is the likely cause. For example, Stat Unit breaks frame time into Game, Draw, G P U, and RHI; if G P U time is dominant, optimizing C P U code won't help. Stat Game lists per-feature timings such as actor ticks, AI, and animation; a high value for an actor tick points you to which code to profile further. A common misconception is to trust perceived slowness: a connected profiler might show the real culprit is the render thread or G P U. Use Stat to triage quickly and avoid premature optimization. Concrete example: add the provided MyPerformanceActor to your level, run Stat Unit, and watch game thread timing rise — that confirms Tick is problematic. Key takeaway: Stat commands are triage tools — use them to form a hypothesis before deeper captures. Stat Commands: Fast runtime checks means run stat unit and stat game first to determine which thread or subsystem is causing slow frames before deeper profiling.. In practical terms, use console stat commands to get immediate timing and thread breakdowns.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Session Frontend is the next step after Stat triage. It records detailed traces over time so you can inspect C P U and G P U work, draw calls, and memory usage. Start by opening Session Frontend from Window → Developer Tools → Session Frontend, connect to your running editor instance, and begin a capture while reproducing the performance issue. The capture collects per-thread timings: Game Thread, Render Thread, RHI Thread, and G P U samples. Use the C P U usage view to sort by self-time or total time to find the function dominating the profile. Drill into the call stack to see which higher-level code called that function. For example, if you find AMyPerformanceActor::Tick has a high self-time, you now have a precise target. A common misconception is to chase high total time functions without checking self-time; prioritize functions with large self-time reductions after optimization. Concrete example: capture a 5–10 second trace while the heavy actor runs, then search for Tick entries and examine the call stack to verify where the heavy loop executes. End by exporting a short clip or saving the capture for comparison after fixes.

Cache locality is a foundational C++ optimization principle you can use to improve C P U efficiency without changing algorithms. Modern CPUs read memory in cache lines. When data that will be used together is stored contiguously, the C P U can load it into cache once and reuse it. This drastically reduces memory access latency compared to chasing pointers that scatter data across memory. In Unreal C++ a common pattern is preferring a TArray of structs over a TArray of pointers to structs when you iterate frequently, because a struct array is contiguous. Concrete example: if you store particle states in a TArray and loop to update them, you get sequential memory access. If instead you store pointers to heap-allocated particle objects, each dereference may miss the cache. A misconception is thinking cache locality only matters for huge systems; in tight per-frame loops it can change your frame time measurably. Key practice: profile hot loops, then consider re-laying out data for contiguous access to reduce cache misses. Cache Locality: the CPU reality means use contiguous containers like tarray of structs to improve cache hit rates in frequently iterated code.. In practical terms, arrange data so related items are contiguous to improve cache hits.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Frequent allocations and deallocations are expensive and can fragment memory or add allocator overhead, especially in tight loops or when many small objects are created per frame. Instead of constructing and destroying objects continuously, object pooling reuses pre-allocated items. For example, projectiles or particles that are spawned and destroyed often benefit from a pool: allocate N objects up front and reuse them by resetting state. This reduces calls to the allocator and keeps memory usage stable. Another practical technique is to prefer stack or contiguous allocations where lifetime and size allow, and use smart pointers like MakeShared selectively rather than in hot loops. A common misconception is that garbage will be cleaned quickly; allocator cost still hits frame timings. Concrete example: change code that calls MakeUnique each spawn into a system that checks out an object from a pool and returns it on deactivate. After pooling, re-profile with Session Frontend to confirm reduced allocator time in C P U traces. Key takeaway: reduce runtime allocations on hot paths to lower frame variance and improve stability. Reducing allocations & Object Pooling means use object pools for frequently created and destroyed instances to avoid allocator overhead and memory fragmentation.. In practical terms, avoid per-frame allocations; reuse memory for frequently created objects.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Per-frame computations are tempting because Tick is easy to use, but unnecessary work in Tick is a common source of slowdowns. Ask whether the computation truly must run every frame. If the value changes rarely, compute it on demand or run it every N frames. If it's independent of frame rate, run it in a timer or a non-tick function. You can also disable ticking by setting PrimaryActorTick. bCanEverTick to false when updates aren't required. A concrete example from the starter actor: heavy trigonometric math inside Tick that repeats every frame can be moved to run once or every tenth frame, or computed asynchronously if appropriate. One misconception is that splitting work across frames always helps; it helps only if the work can be distributed without changing game semantics. After making a change, re-run Stat Unit and capture a Session Frontend trace to verify that Game thread time decreases. Key takeaway: reduce per-frame work by moving calculations to less frequent events or disabling Tick entirely when possible. Avoid unnecessary per-frame computations means only put truly frame-dependent work in tick. prefer timers, events, or conditional execution for expensive calculations.. In practical terms, don't do work every tick; move work to events or lower frequency updates.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Const correctness is both a correctness and an optimization aid. Marking functions and parameters as const communicates intent, makes A P I contracts clearer, and can help the compiler produce better code in optimized builds. When you promise not to mutate data you enable safer reasoning about side effects, and you often let the optimizer perform more aggressive inlining or reordering. Use const references to avoid unnecessary copies of large structs passed into functions. A practical example: change a function that takes a large struct by value into taking const MyStruct& to remove a copy per call in a hot loop. Keep in mind this is not a substitute for measuring: while const can reduce copies, moving to contiguous data and reducing allocations are often larger wins. A common misconception is over-using const everywhere expecting huge performance gains; const helps correctness and can reduce some overhead, but profiling remains the source of truth. Key takeaway: use const for clarity and to remove accidental copies in hot code paths. Const correctness & compiler help means const references and const methods reduce accidental copies and help maintain clear, optimizable code in hot paths.. In practical terms, use const and clear interfaces so the compiler can optimize and you reduce bugs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Debugging C++ in Unreal requires the right build configuration and workflow. Always use DebugGame Editor or Development Editor builds when you need to step through code; Release builds strip symbols and prevent meaningful stepping. To start, attach your IDE debugger to the Unreal Editor process or to a standalone game. Set breakpoints at suspected locations; conditional breakpoints reduce noise by only breaking when a condition is true. Use Step Over to execute the current line, Step Into to dive into called functions, and Step Out to return. Watch windows let you monitor variable values across steps, and the call stack shows the sequence of functions that led to the current point — this is essential when investigating crashes or unexpected states. A common error is debugging the wrong build configuration or forgetting to rebuild after code changes, which leads to mismatched symbols. UE_LOG is the recommended way to emit structured messages in Unreal C++. Unlike ad-hoc prints, UE_LOG supports log categories and verbosity levels so you can filter and control output both in the editor and in standalone logs. Define a custom category with DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY_STATIC to group messages from a subsystem, then use verbosity such as Error, Warning, Display, Log, Verbose, or VeryVerbose to mark importance. For infrequent issues, Verbose or VeryVerbose is appropriate; these levels are commonly ignored in shipping configurations to avoid performance cost and log noise. Example usage: UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("My variable value: %f"), MyVariable); or define a category and log there. A common mistake is leaving heavy logging enabled in hot loops; logging itself can slow your game and flood storage. Use UE_LOG sparingly in hot paths or gate it behind conditional checks. Finally, logs appear in the Output Log and saved game logs, making them invaluable for diagnosing crashes that are hard to reproduce in the editor. These are the core concepts you should retain. First, Stat commands provide immediate triage information — use Stat FPS, Stat Unit, and Stat Game to spot which subsystem needs attention. Second, Session Frontend gives function-level timings and call stacks so you can find hot functions and understand why they are expensive. Third, cache locality matters: contiguous data access reduces cache misses and is especially important for tight per-frame loops. Fourth, reduce allocations by using object pools for frequently created objects to avoid allocator overhead. Fifth, avoid unnecessary computations in Tick; prefer events, timers, or lower-frequency updates. Sixth, use const correctness to avoid accidental copies and make code clearer. Seventh, debug with the appropriate build configurations and use breakpoints, stepping, watches, and the call stack to inspect runtime problems. Finally, use UE_LOG with categories and verbosity to produce structured, filterable logs. Keep profiling-driven changes small and re-verify with captures.

Here are three practical reminders to use immediately. First, measure before you change: start with Stat and then capture Session Frontend; targeting the wrong subsystem wastes time. Second, optimize memory and frequency: prefer contiguous data and reduce allocations, and move heavy work out of Tick or execute it less often. Third, debug and log wisely: attach a DebugGame Editor build to step through code, use conditional breakpoints and watch windows, and use UE_LOG categories with Verbose levels for deep traces that can be filtered. These three habits — measure, change small, and verify — prevent wasted effort and regressions while improving performance reliably.
